slides.label: The Curvature of a Spike
slides.notes: Chapter 14, printed pages 143 through 148 and PDF pages 172 through 177, asks how curvature can be visible everywhere and yet numerically live at one point. The guiding model is a cone or polyhedral spike: away from the vertex the surface is locally flat, but a loop around the vertex returns with a missing angle.

slides.label: The Angular Ledger
slides.notes: The cone replaces smooth curvature density with an angular ledger. Around an ordinary planar point the incident angle is two pi. Around a spike the available angle is smaller, and the shortfall is the total Gaussian curvature stored at the vertex. This is the discrete version of integrating K over a tiny neighborhood.

slides.label: Unroll the Cone
slides.notes: Unrolling the cone is the cleanest intrinsic test because it avoids looking from outside. Cut along a generator and flatten the surface. The sides fit in the plane without stretching, but the circular neighborhood opens into a sector whose missing wedge is exactly the defect. The vertex remembers the cut even after every other point becomes flat.

slides.label: Curvature as a Point Measure
slides.notes: Smooth Gaussian curvature spreads through area; spike curvature is concentrated like a point mass. We should not say the cone has an ordinary finite value of K at the tip. Instead its integral over any small disk containing the tip is the defect, while disks missing the tip integrate to zero.

slides.label: Polyhedral Vertex Formula
slides.notes: For a polyhedral surface the same bookkeeping is local and finite. Add the face angles that meet at one vertex, subtract the sum from two pi, and obtain the vertex curvature. Positive defect looks like a peak; negative defect looks like excess angle or a saddle-like vertex. The formula is entirely intrinsic because it uses face angles measured on the surface.

slides.label: Spherical Image of the Normal Fan
slides.notes: The extrinsic view follows the normals. Around a smooth patch, the Gauss map sweeps out area on the unit sphere; for a polyhedral vertex, each face contributes one constant normal and the normals trace a spherical polygon. The area of that spherical polygon equals the same defect, so the normal picture agrees with the angle-sum ledger.

slides.label: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Agreement
slides.notes: This slide is the conceptual hinge: the angular defect is computed by a traveler confined to the surface, while the spherical image uses the surface as embedded in space. Their equality is the polyhedral shadow of the Theorema Egregium. Curvature is revealed by embedding, but its value is already encoded in the intrinsic metric.

slides.label: The Smoothing Limit
slides.notes: A spike can be rounded into a smooth cap, and then the curvature density becomes ordinary again. As the cap shrinks, the pointwise curvature grows while the area supporting it shrinks. The important invariant is the integral: the total curvature tends to the same angular defect rather than disappearing or exploding.

slides.label: Worked Defect Computation
slides.notes: A quick computation makes the unit of measurement concrete. If five equilateral triangle corners meet at a vertex, the angle sum is five pi over three, so the defect is pi over three. If six meet, the defect is zero and the surface is locally flat like a hexagonal tiling. If seven meet, the defect is negative.

slides.label: Recap and Next Step
slides.notes: The chapter turns curvature into finite accounting. Cone tips, polyhedral vertices, spherical images, and smoothing limits all tell the same story: Gaussian curvature can concentrate, and its integral is stable under the modeling choice. This prepares the next discussion, where shape-operator and curvature ideas become sharper local tools.
